paras: The lynching of Henry Ivy and Sim Acoff took place in the early morning of April 13, 1882, when about forty masked men took the two Black prisoners from their guards at a school house near Brown's Station, Dallas County, Alabama. Ivy was found hanging from a tree, and Acoff's body was reported found in a swamp eleven days later, a report that was denied and then repeated. The papers presented the killing as a sequel to the murder of planter J. B. Weisinger, for which two other men had already been executed.

J. B. Weisinger, a planter of about 60, was killed in his house near Brown's Station on December 19, 1881, and half a dozen Black men were suspected of a part in it. Bill Ludlow and Al Weissinger were convicted and executed at Selma on March 31, still protesting their innocence.

On a Wednesday afternoon, Henry Ivy confessed that he had done the killing, naming his brother Porter Ivy, said to be serving a life sentence, and Acoff, who was then at large on the plantation. Most accounts said the confession was made to seven white men, though the Ottawa Free Trader said seven "colored" men. Ivy and Acoff were arrested and taken before 'Squire Gwynn, who held them for the grand jury.

News of the confession "greatly excited" Black people on nearby plantations, and white residents were said to have stopped them from hanging the prisoners on the spot. The prisoners were given to three white guards, who took them to a school house for the night.

At about 2 a.m., while one guard was away getting water, forty masked men, "thought to be all whites," rode up, bound and gagged the guards, and rode off with the prisoners, who begged for "just one more day" of life. Black men passing through the woods near the school house found Ivy's body hanging from a tree limb on Thursday evening. The New York special placed the lynching in woods four miles south of Brown's Station on the Alabama Central Railroad.

Acoff's body was not found at first, though the special said "there can be no doubt he has been killed." A Selma dispatch of April 24 said his body had been found in a swamp near where Ivy was hanged, with buzzards feeding on it and bullet holes in the head; the report had been denied but was asserted again. An "old and highly respectable citizen" of Brown's Station, suspected of knowing the details, showed Ivy's written confession to a correspondent and said that calling the men lynched would not be "far wrong." No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The story reached the white press through a Selma wire dated April 14 and a longer New York special, printed from Washington to Sacramento on April 14 and 15. Headlines were brief, such as "Lynched" and "Lynched in Alabama," but the Sacramento Record-Union used "Murderers Lynched in Alabama" and the Dallas Herald's front page called the victims "Ebony Fiends." Several wire versions added that this made "five men hanged for that murder," counting the two executions.

Weekly papers then carried shortened briefs, some of which dropped details or introduced errors. The Brookhaven Ledger said the men were taken "from jail," and a brief in the Gloucester County Democrat, also printed in Rhode Island and South Carolina, made them brothers and moved the event to "Selma, Mo."

The fullest account, in the Morning Journal and Courier on April 25, ran under a headline suggesting two innocent men had been hanged, yet closed by noting that the lynchers "did their work thoroughly."

Acoff's first name appears as Jim, Sim and Tim, and the Dallas Herald printed "Scoff" and "Scott." Most reports put the lynching on the night of April 12-13, but the Evening Star said "Wednesday morning," the Savannah Morning News later said "the 14th," and the Richmond Dispatch "the 4th." The Ottawa Free Trader alone said both bodies were found next day hanging from two trees in the road, unlike the Selma reports, which said Acoff's body was missing and later found shot in a swamp.

bases: About forty masked men took two Black prisoners held for the grand jury from their guards and hanged Henry Ivy; his companion was reported killed (A3, A14, A16).

Ivy was taken from guards by about forty masked men and found hanged from a tree, punished for a murder he had confessed before any grand jury acted (A3, A4, A14); Acoff's death is reported but less firmly (A15, A16).

A Selma wire, a New York special and a longer separate account agree that masked men took Ivy and Acoff from guards and that Ivy was found hanged (A3, A4, A14); only Acoff's fate is contested (A12, A15).

accounts.label: Selma wire and New York special
accounts.gist: Forty masked men, largely or all white, overpowered the guards at the school house at 2 a.m. and rode off with the two men; Ivy was found hanging nearby and Acoff's body had not been found.

accounts.label: Longer correspondent's account
accounts.gist: Adds the background of the executions, the hearing before 'Squire Gwynn, the three white guards, a respectable citizen's hint that the men were lynched, and the discovery of Ivy's body by Black passers-by Thursday evening.

accounts.label: Ottawa Free Trader digest
accounts.gist: Says the confession was made to seven 'colored' men, the mob came at midnight, and both bodies were found next day hanging from two trees in the road.

accounts.label: Selma dispatch, April 24
accounts.gist: Acoff's body was reported found in a swamp near where Ivey was hung, with bullet-holes in the head; the report was denied but reasserted.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Selma wire or New York special under 'Lynched' or 'Lynched in Alabama', treating the confession as settling guilt.
The Sacramento Record-Union headed it 'Murderers Lynched in Alabama' and the Dallas Herald 'A Couple of Ebony Fiends Lynched in Alabama'.

The Morning Journal and Courier headline stressed that two men protesting innocence had already been hanged, while calling the victims 'scoundrels' in a quoted remark and praising the lynchers' thoroughness.
The Ottawa Free Trader grouped it with other cases under 'Thriving Business of Judge Lynch'.
